entry: Central tradition of Western plainchant: monophonic, unaccompanied sacred song in [[Latin]] of the Roman [[Catholic Church]]. It developed mainly in western and central Europe during the 9th and 10th centuries. Although popular legend credits [[Pope Gregory I]] with its invention, scholars believe he only ordered a compilation of melodies, largely a later Carolingian synthesis. Gregorian chants were organized into four, then eight, and finally 12 modes, and were written in neumes, an early form of [[Musical notation|musical notation]]. Multi-voice elaborations, known as organum, were an early stage in the development of Western polyphony. Traditionally sung by [[Choir|choirs]] of men and boys in churches, it is the music of the Roman Rite, performed at Mass and in the monastic Office. Ambrosian chant still continues in use in [[Milan]].

American actor. A popular film star from the 1940s to the 1970s, he was named the 12th-greatest male star of Classic Hollywood Cinema by the American Film Institute in 1999. After studying with Sanford Meisner at the Neighborhood Playhouse, he gained critical success in *The Keys of the Kingdom* (1944), which earned his first Academy Award nomination. He reached global recognition in the 1950s and 1960s, starring in *The Snows of Kilimanjaro* (1952) with [[Ava Gardner]] and *Roman Holiday* (1953) with [[Audrey Hepburn]]. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for playing Atticus Finch in *To Kill a Mockingbird* (1962). He was also active in politics, challenging the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1947, and was regarded as a political opponent by [[Richard Nixon]]. [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1969.

Early Christian theologian and orator, archbishop of [[Constantinople]]. He is widely considered the most accomplished rhetorical stylist of the patristic age. Classically trained in rhetoric and philosophy, he infused Hellenism into the early Church and established the paradigm for later Byzantine theologians and church officials. He made a significant impact on Trinitarian theology among both Greek and Latin-speaking theologians, and is remembered as the "Trinitarian Theologian". With [[Basil of Caesarea]] and [[Gregory of Nyssa]], he is known as one of the [[Cappadocia|Cappadocian]] Fathers. He is a saint in both Eastern and Western Christianity: the [[Catholic Church]] numbers him among the Doctors of the Church, and the [[Eastern Orthodox Church]] honors him as one of the Three Holy Hierarchs.

Early Christian theologian and bishop of Nyssa. He served as bishop from 372 to 376 and again from 378 until his death. With his elder brother [[Basil of Caesarea]] and their friend [[Gregory of Nazianzus]], he is known as one of the Cappadocian Fathers. He lacked his brother's administrative ability but made significant contributions to the doctrine of the [[Trinity]] and the [[Nicene Creed]]. His philosophical writings were influenced by [[Origen]], and since the mid-twentieth century scholars have increasingly studied his work on universal salvation, challenging many traditional interpretations of his theology. He is credited with being the first person in recorded history to write against all forms of slavery, declaring the institution inherently sinful. He is venerated as a saint by the [[Catholic Church]], Eastern Orthodoxy, Oriental Orthodox Churches, [[Anglicanism]] and Lutheranism.

Archipelagic country of the West Indies in the eastern [[Caribbean Sea]] (pop., 2026: 117,362). It consists of the island of Grenada, the smaller islands of Carriacou and Petite Martinique, and part of the Grenadines; its area is 344 sq km, and its capital is St. George's. The island was sighted by [[Christopher Columbus]] in 1498 and ceded to the British under the Treaty of Paris on February 10, 1763. Independence came on February 7, 1974, under Eric Gairy, and the country joined the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] with [[Elizabeth II]] as head of state. In 1979 the New JEWEL Movement overthrew Gairy's government, and Maurice Bishop led a People's Revolutionary Government until his execution; a U.S.-led invasion followed in October 1983. The current head of state is King [[Charles III]], represented by a governor-general.

Small [[Explosive|explosive]] projectile, thrown by hand or launched by a rifle attachment or dedicated launcher. A modern hand grenade contains an explosive charge (filler), a detonator, an internal striker and an arming safety. Once the user removes the transport safety pin and the grenade leaves the hand, a fuze burns down to the detonator. Grenades disperse fragments, shockwaves, chemical aerosols, fire or a jet of metal. Stick grenades, with a handle for leverage, have been considered obsolete by Western countries since [[World War II]] and the [[Cold War]]. The English word may come from the French for "[[Pomegranate|pomegranate]]" or from Latin *granatus*, "filled with grain." Rudimentary incendiary grenades appeared in the [[Byzantine Empire]], which threw [[Greek fire]] in stone and ceramic jars. The [[Joseon]] Dynasty first used a "flying impact thunder crash bomb" on September 1, 1592, during the Japanese invasions of Korea.

Swedish and American film actress. A leading star during Hollywood's [[Silent film|silent]] and early golden eras, she launched her career in the 1924 Swedish film *The Saga of Gösta Berling*. [[Louis B. Mayer]] of [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer|MGM]] brought her to Hollywood in 1925, and *Flesh and the Devil* (1926) made her an international star. Her first sound film, *Anna Christie* (1930), was promoted with the tagline "Garbo talks!" Many critics and film historians consider her performance in *Camille* (1936) her finest, and it earned her a third Academy Award nomination. After a turn to comedy in *Ninotchka* (1939), she retired from films; *Two-Faced Woman* (1941) was the last of her 28 feature films. She later shunned publicity and became an art collector whose holdings included works by [[Pierre-Auguste Renoir]]. In 1954 she received an Academy Honorary Award.

Swedish climate activist. In 2018, at age 15, she began a solo school strike outside the Swedish parliament, an action that inspired the worldwide Fridays for Future movement. She broadened her focus to human rights, voicing support for Ukraine, Palestine, Armenia, Cuba and Western Sahara. In 2025 she twice joined a humanitarian flotilla bound for the [[Gaza Strip]]. Supporters credit her with increasing public attention to climate issues, while critics have questioned her rhetoric, methods and role in political debate. She was named [[Time (magazine)|Time]]'s Person of the Year in 2019.

Neutral, achromatic color intermediate between [[Black|black]] and [[White|white]]. It is the color of a rain or storm cloud, of ash and of [[Lead|lead]]. The first recorded use of gray as a color name in English was in 700. Grey is the dominant spelling in European and Commonwealth English, while gray is more common in American English. In Europe and North America, surveys associate gray most often with neutrality, [[Conformity|conformity]], [[Boredom|boredom]], uncertainty, [[Old age|old age]], indifference and humility, and only one percent of respondents chose it as their favorite color. In antiquity and the Middle Ages, gray was the color of undyed wool and was worn by peasants, as well as by Cistercian monks and Franciscan friars as a symbol of humility and poverty. It became the most common background for the portraits of [[Rembrandt]] and for many paintings by [[El Greco]].

American medical drama television series. Its title combines the protagonist's surname with *Gray's Anatomy*, a classic textbook of human anatomy. Developed by [[Shonda Rhimes]], it follows surgical interns, residents and attendings at the fictional Seattle Grace Hospital. It premiered on the [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] network on March 27, 2005, and is the longest-running scripted primetime show currently airing on ABC. Set in Seattle, Washington, it is filmed primarily in [[Los Angeles]]. Its spin-offs include *Private Practice* and *Station 19*, and the series has received numerous Primetime Emmy Award nominations.

Ancient breed of [[Dog|dog]] and sighthound, historically developed for hunting game by sight and speed. Greyhounds are tall, muscular and smooth-coated, with a flexible, S-shaped outline. They are used in organized coursing and racing, and are also kept as show dogs and companion animals. In racing, Greyhounds can reach peak speeds of at least 69 km/h (43 mph). A 2008 [[University of Pennsylvania]] study found them among the least aggressive breeds toward strangers, owners and other dogs. They are generally gentle and affectionate, though small animals such as [[Cat|cats]] may trigger prey-driven behavior.

Response to the loss of something deemed important, in particular the [[Death|death]] of a person or animal to which a bond or affection was formed. Although conventionally focused on emotion, grief also has physical, cognitive, social, cultural, spiritual and political dimensions. Bereavement describes the state of loss, while grief is the reaction to it. Losses such as [[Unemployment|unemployment]], ill health or the end of a relationship also cause grief. It can appear as [[Sadness|sadness]], [[Anger|anger]], [[Anxiety|anxiety]], laughter or even numbness, and most people show natural resilience. Modern research has moved beyond rigid stage models toward more flexible frameworks. The death of a spouse, child or parent carries higher risks of [[Depression (mood)|depression]].

Legendary creature with the body, tail and back legs of a [[Lion|lion]] and the head and wings of an [[Eagle|eagle]]. Greek and Roman texts associated griffins with the gold deposits of [[Central Asia]], and [[Herodotus]] and [[Aeschylus]] preserved the earliest classical writings on the topic. Because the lion was considered king of beasts and the eagle king of birds, the griffin was thought especially powerful in the [[Middle Ages]]. [[Pliny the Elder]] was the first to state explicitly that griffins were winged, and Isidore of Seville, writing in the 7th century, called them a great enemy of [[Horse|horses]].

Russian mystic and faith healer. Born a peasant in the [[Siberia|Siberian]] village of Pokrovskoye, he gained a reputation as a starets after a religious conversion on a [[Pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] to a monastery in 1897. He traveled to [[Saint Petersburg]], and in November 1905 he met [[Nicholas II]] and Empress Alexandra Feodorovna. From late 1906 he acted as a faith healer for the couple's son, Alexei, who had hemophilia. Some saw him as a mystic and prophet, and others as a religious charlatan. His influence peaked in 1915, when Nicholas left to oversee the army in [[World War I]]. He was assassinated by conservative nobles who opposed his influence over the imperial family. Historians often suggest that his reputation helped discredit the Tsarist government, precipitating the overthrow of the [[House of Romanov]] shortly afterward.

Form of [[Cooking|cooking]] that applies heat to the surface of food, commonly from above, below or the side. Grilling usually involves significant direct, radiant heat and is used to cook meat and vegetables quickly. Outdoor grilling often uses [[Charcoal|charcoal]], wood or propane gas; in the United States, grilling with the heat source above is called broiling. Direct heat can expose food to temperatures often in excess of 260 °C (500 °F), and the [[Maillard reaction]] that gives grilled meat its roast flavor occurs only above 155 °C (310 °F). Large, tough cuts of meat are unsuitable, since the fast technique would not allow the meat to cook slowly and tenderize. Cooking beef, pork, poultry and fish at high temperatures can form [[Carcinogen|carcinogens]] such as heterocyclic amines, though marination may reduce them.

German collection of [[Fairy tale|fairy tales]] by the [[Brothers Grimm]], Jacob and Wilhelm, originally titled *Kinder- und Hausmärchen* (Children's and Household Tales). The first volume, published in 1812, contained 86 stories, and a second volume of 70 more followed in 1815. By the seventh edition in 1857, the collection had grown to 200 tales and 10 "Children's Legends". Although called "Children's Tales", the early volumes were regarded as unsuitable for children because of their scholarly content and subject matter. Later editions removed sexual references and changed the wicked mother in [[Hansel and Gretel]] to a stepmother, although violence became more prevalent in punishing villains. The collection is considered the seminal work of Western [[Children's literature|children's literature]] and is listed by [[UNESCO]] in its Memory of the World Register.

Population or subspecies of [[Brown bear|brown bear]] inhabiting [[North America]]. Brown bears first migrated there from [[Eurasia]] between about 177,000 and 111,000 BP, and most grizzlies descend from that initial population. In the 19th century the grizzly was classified as 86 distinct species, but modern genetic testing shows it to be a subspecies of the brown bear. Around 30,000 grizzlies live in [[Alaska]], while fewer than 2,000 remain in the lower 48 states. Its omnivorous diet includes [[Salmon|salmon]] and vegetation.

Junctional area between the torso and the thigh, also called the inguinal region. It lies on either side of the pubic tubercle and is marked by a crease, the inguinal groove. The adductor muscles bring the thigh toward the midline. Three to five deep inguinal lymph nodes play a role in the [[Immune system|immune system]]. The inguinal ligament runs from the pubic tubercle to the anterior superior iliac spine and is important in [[Hernia|hernia]] surgery. An inguinal hernia is a hernia of the groin, and a strained adductor muscle is a common sports injury.

Monetary measure of the total market value of all final goods and services produced by a country or countries in a specific period, usually a year. It is often used to measure economic activity and to compare economies internationally. Its major components are consumption, government spending, net exports and investment. Simon Kuznets developed the modern concept for a 1934 report to the [[United States|U.S.]] Congress and warned against its use as a measure of welfare. The United States switched from gross national product to GDP in 1991. Because it does not account for how income is distributed, GDP does not measure living standards or [[Well-being|well-being]] directly, and figures are often adjusted by [[Purchasing power parity|purchasing power parity]] for cross-country comparisons. Critics note that it omits resource extraction, environmental impact and unpaid domestic work, and alternatives such as the [[Human Development Index]] have been proposed. The [[OECD]] and the [[International Monetary Fund]] maintain their own definitions.

Category of plant tissues that are neither dermal nor [[Vascular tissue|vascular]], forming the bulk of the plant body. Ground tissue is one of three main tissue systems, alongside the protective and vascular systems, and it provides structural support, storage, metabolic activity and [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. Its cells are classified by their [[Cell wall|cell walls]]. Parenchyma cells have thin primary walls, usually remain alive at maturity and form the filler tissue of soft parts; they store starch in roots, [[Potato|tubers]] and [[Cereal|cereal]] seed endosperm, and their large central [[Vacuole|vacuoles]] store water and ions. Collenchyma cells provide extra support in regions of new growth. Sclerenchyma cells have thick lignified walls, often die at maturity and provide the main structural support. Aerenchyma, with large air cavities, helps aquatic plants float.

Large burrowing [[Rodent|rodent]] of North America, also called the woodchuck. A member of the [[Marmot|marmot]] group of large ground squirrels, it is found through much of the Eastern United States, across [[Canada]] and into [[Alaska]]. Unlike most marmots, which live in rocky and mountainous areas, it is a lowland animal. It is considered one of the most solitary marmot species, although social organization and pair bonds vary across populations. It is a crucial habitat engineer, as its burrowing maintains healthy soil in woodlands and plains. It is also extremely intelligent, forming complex social networks and whistling to warn of threats.

1993 American fantasy romantic comedy film directed by Harold Ramis. [[Bill Murray]] stars as a cynical television weatherman trapped in a time loop while covering the annual Groundhog Day event in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania. It was released by [[Columbia Pictures]] and earned over $105 million. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry in 2006. The term groundhog day, meaning a monotonous, repetitive situation, has become part of the English lexicon.

Water located beneath Earth's surface in [[Soil|soil]] and [[Rock (geology)|rock]] pore spaces and rock fractures. About 30 percent of all readily available fresh water in the world is groundwater. An [[Aquifer|aquifer]] is a unit of rock or sediment that can yield a usable quantity of water. Groundwater is often cheaper, more convenient and less vulnerable to pollution than surface water, so it supplies many public drinking water systems; over 2 billion people rely on it as their primary source. In the [[United States]], groundwater provides the largest source of usable water storage, and [[California]] withdraws the largest amount of any state. Polluted groundwater is harder to clean up than river or lake pollution, with sources including [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], pesticides and [[Landfill|landfills]]. Overpumping can cause land subsidence, as in sinking cities such as [[Bangkok]].

Set with an associative operation, an identity element and an inverse for every element. For example, the [[Integer|integers]] form a group under addition. The concept was developed to treat numbers, geometric shapes and polynomial roots in a unified way, and some authors regard it as a central organizing principle of contemporary mathematics. In geometry, the symmetries of an object form a group, and Lie groups appear in the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics. The Poincaré group consists of the symmetries of spacetime in [[Special relativity|special relativity]]. The concept arose in the study of polynomial equations, when [[Évariste Galois]] introduced the term in the 1830s for the symmetry group of an equation's roots. Modern [[Group theory|group theory]] studies groups in their own right, using subgroups, quotient groups and simple groups.

Column of elements in the [[Periodic table|periodic table]], also known as a family. Elements in a group share similar characteristics because their outermost [[Electron shell|electron shells]] are alike, and most chemical properties depend on the location of the outermost electron. The 18 numbered groups follow a system recommended by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry in 1988, though older numbering schemes assign some numbers differently. Some groups have traditional names: group 16 is the "oxygen group" or the "chalcogens", and the "iron group" usually refers to group 8.
